proof_text:
If $x = u$ and $y = v$, then
$\{\{x\}, \{x, y\}\} = \{\{u\}, \{u, v\}\}$ trivially. Conversely,
suppose $\{\{x\}, \{x, y\}\} = \{\{u\}, \{u, v\}\}$. The intersection
of all members of the left set is $\{x\}$, and of the right set is
$\{u\}$, which forces $\{x\} = \{u\}$ and hence $x = u$. Now consider
two cases:
1. If $x = y$, then the left set is $\{\{x\}, \{x\}\} = \{\{x\}\}$,
   meaning the right set must also be a singleton. Thus
   $\{u\} = \{u, v\}$, which forces $u = v$, yielding $x = y = u = v$.
2. If $x \neq y$, then the left set contains a unique two-element
   member $\{x, y\}$, which must equal the unique two-element member
   $\{u, v\}$ on the right. Since $x = u$ and $x \neq y$, it follows
   that $y = v$.

Theorem:
given: x, y, u, v is \set
then: \pair:of{x, y} = \pair:of{u, v}
iff:
. x = u
. y = v
Documented:
. called: "coordinate equality for ordered pairs"
. description: "Kuratowski ordered pairs are equal exactly when their
                corresponding coordinates are equal."
